food.text: Tuscany's famous plain, unsalted white bread traces its origin to the 16th century, when salt was heavily taxed. It became a bread that accompanies all foods in Tuscan cooking.
The colonization of the Americas brought potatoes, tomatoes, capsicums and maize to Italy, significantly changing Italian cuisine. Sugar beet followed, introduced in quantity in the 18th century.

Europeans met tea, coffee and drinking chocolate in the early modern period, but all three only became popular social drinks in the 17th century. Chocolate was first to catch on, and it was one of the preferred drinks of the Spanish nobility in the 16th and early 17th century.

Bartolomeo Scappi, chef to Pope Pius IV in the Vatican kitchen, became famous for his cookbook Opera dell'arte del cucinare, published in 1570. It lists approximately 1,000 recipes of Renaissance cuisine and gives the first known picture of a fork.

Cristoforo di Messisbugo, steward to Ippolito d'Este, published Banchetti compositioni di vivande in 1549. The book includes pies and tarts with 124 recipes for various fillings, and it emphasises Eastern spices and sugar.

In 1662, Bartolomeo Stefani, chef to the Gonzagas, published the last Italian high-cuisine cookbook, L'Arte di Ben Cucinare. It introduced vitto ordinario, or ordinary food, to Italian cookery, as Italy turned toward regionalism and simple cooking.
In 1790, Francesco Leonardi's book L'Apicio moderno sketched a history of Italian cuisine from the Roman Age. It also gave the first recipe of a tomato-based sauce.

Corrado's 1798 cookbook edition added a Treatise on the Potato, after the Frenchman Antoine-Augustin Parmentier successfully promoted the tuber. His book also included a tomato soup similar to today's Tuscan pappa al pomodoro.

In the 18th century, Italian cookbooks began to show regional cooking and were addressed to bourgeois housewives rather than professional chefs. La cuoca cremonese, written in 1794, arranged ingredients by season with chapters on meat, fish and vegetables.

Sfogliatella Santa Rosa, the ancestor of today's sfogliatella, was created in the 17th century in the monastery of Santa Rosa in Conca dei Marini, Campania. Pasquale Pintauro, a Naples pastry chef, acquired the original recipe and began selling the pastries in his shop in 1818.

Domenico Romoli's cookbook Panunto made a virtue of seasonal necessity by including a recipe for each day of the year. Chefs and doctors still described foods by their effects on the four humours, as heating or cooling, moistening or drying.

art.text: Italy was the main centre of artistic innovation during the Italian Renaissance, culminating in the High Renaissance with artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, and Antonello da Messina. These artists influenced Mannerism, the next phase of Renaissance art.

Italy kept its artistic prominence into the 17th century during the Baroque period and into the 18th century with the emergence of Neoclassicism. Both movements originated in Rome and spread throughout Western art.

Italian architecture gave the world Palladianism, a style that inspired Neoclassical architecture. It also influenced the designs noblemen used for country houses all over the world, notably in the United Kingdom, Australia and the United States, from the late 17th century onward.

Italy was the main centre of artistic developments throughout the Renaissance and kept its artistic dominance into the 17th century with the Baroque. Both the Baroque and Neoclassicism originated in Rome and were the last Italian-born styles that spread to all Western art.

Instruments such as the piano and violin were invented in Italy. Many classical music forms, including the symphony, concerto and sonata, trace their roots to innovations in 16th and 17th century Italian music.

Michelangelo was a master of painting, sculpture, architecture, and poetry. His statue of David, made between 1501 and 1504, conveys both physical beauty and intense psychological depth. It is one of the works showing his skill in portraying the human body.

Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512. The frescoes depict Biblical and classical subjects, and they are renowned for their powerful representation of the human form and spiritual intensity. The ceiling is regarded as one of the most celebrated masterpieces of Western art.

In the late 18th century, Italy was affected by the Neoclassical movement, and villas, palaces, gardens, interiors and art began to be based on ancient Roman and Greek themes. Buildings were widely themed on the Villa Capra "La Rotonda", the masterpiece by Andrea Palladio.

In the 1750s Giovanni Paolo Panini painted a trio of almost identical paintings called Ancient Rome for his patron, the comte de Stainville. They show sites and sculptures such as the Colosseum, the Pantheon, Laocoön and His Sons, and the Apollo Belvedere. Panini painted himself behind Stainville's armchair.

Rome is famous for huge squares, many built in the 17th century, including Piazza Navona and Piazza di Spagna. One of the most emblematic examples of baroque art there is the Fontana di Trevi by Nicola Salvi.

The discoveries of the lost cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum changed Neoclassical design in Italy. Before them, buildings were themed on Ancient Rome and Classical Athens, but afterwards they were inspired by these archaeological sites.

The two-shell dome of the Royal Chapel of the Treasure of St. Januarius in Naples was built between 1608 and 1618. Iron chains were incorporated into its structure, with the first placed during construction in 1612. Two more chains were added after earthquakes in 1626 and 1627.
tags: Royal Chapel of the Treasure of St. Januarius

art.text: Authentic East Asian lacquered ware, including Japanese work, made its way into Europe by the 17th century. In the late 17th century, high European demand and rumors that East Asian makers kept their best work for home markets led to imitation pieces, starting in Italy. This imitation finish became known as japanning.

The Naples chapel dome kept cracking, so in 1724 the internal masonry lantern connecting the inner and outer domes was removed to lighten the structure. A wooden and iron truss was added between the shells. A lighter wooden structure replaced the exterior lantern between 1724 and 1726.
tags: Royal Chapel of the Treasure of St. Januarius

art.text: In Spain, false vaults made of wood or reed and covered with plaster were used in chapel domes. They gave the appearance of stone construction.

war.text: After 1503, most of the fighting in the Italian Wars was started by French invasions of Lombardy and Piedmont. The French were able to hold territory for periods of time, but they could not do so permanently.

The Italian Wars ended with the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, under which France was largely expelled from Italy. In exchange France gained Calais from England, while Spain acquired sovereignty over the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily.

On 6 May 1527, mutinous troops of Charles V captured Rome. The Imperial army of 14,000 Germans, including Lutherans, 6,000 Spaniards and some Italians was largely unpaid. Despite orders not to storm the city, it broke into the scarcely defended city and began looting, killing and holding citizens for ransom without any restraint. After some 1,000 defenders were executed the pillage began: women were raped, hospice patients killed, monks castrated, nuns raped, and priests targeted for killing.
tags: War of the League of Cognac

war.text: Infantry changed profoundly during the Italian Wars, moving from a force of pikes and halberds to a more flexible mix of arquebusiers, pikemen and other troops. The Italian War of 1521 demonstrated the power of massed firearms in pike and shot formations.

During the sack of Rome, the Swiss Guard were almost annihilated making their last stand in the Teutonic Cemetery within the Vatican; their captain, Kaspar Röist, was wounded and later killed by Spanish soldiers in front of his wife in his house. Those who fell back toward St. Peter's Basilica were massacred, and only 42 survived. Pope Clement VII took refuge in Castel Sant'Angelo after the Swiss Guard were annihilated in a delaying rear guard action, and he remained there a prisoner until a ransom was paid to the pillagers. On 6 June he surrendered and agreed to pay 400,000 ducati in exchange for his life.
In April 1528 a French expeditionary force, supported by a Genoese fleet, besieged Naples. Disease forced the French to withdraw in August, and both sides were now anxious to end the war.

After another French defeat at Landriano on 21 June 1529, Francis agreed to the Treaty of Cambrai with Charles in August. It was called the "Peace of the Ladies" because it was negotiated by Francis's mother, Louise of Savoy, and Charles's aunt Margaret.

Naples was one of the places where war brought hardship. When the Austrians arrived in 1707, the Neapolitan aristocracy welcomed them. But while the war raged, Austria imposed huge tax burdens on the city and did not provide adequate administration until peace returned.

An estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people were murdered in the sack of Rome; it is said that two thousand bodies were disposed of in the Tiber River. Many Imperial soldiers also died afterward, largely from diseases caused by masses of unburied corpses in the streets. Rome's population dropped from 55,000 to 10,000 because of atrocities, famine, plague and flight from the city. Pillaging ended in February 1528, when the food supply ran out, there was no one left to ransom and plague appeared, and the spread of plague and the approach of League forces under Marshal Odet de Foix forced the army to withdraw toward Naples. Benvenuto Cellini, an eyewitness, described the sack in his works.

Emperor Charles V professed great embarrassment that his troops had imprisoned Pope Clement. He eventually restored many of the spoils of the sack, valued at more than 4 million ducati, to the Vatican, and came to terms with the Pope in the Treaty of Barcelona in 1529.

Cosimo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, defeated a French army at Marciano on 2 August 1554. Siena held out until April 1555 but was then absorbed by Florence, and in 1569 it became part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

In 1553 a Franco-Ottoman force captured the Genoese island of Corsica. In the same year, French-backed Tuscan exiles, supported by Catherine de' Medici, seized control of Siena, which brought France into conflict with Florence.

literature.text: Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote has been called "the first novel" by many literary scholars. It was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, and might be viewed as a parody of chivalric romance such as Le Morte d'Arthur. Satirising earlier writings was only made possible by the printing press.

Italian writers pioneered the fairy tale genre. Giovanni Francesco Straparola's The Facetious Nights of Straparola (1550 to 1555) and Giambattista Basile's Pentamerone (1634) are among the earliest printed fairy tales in Europe.

Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote de la Mancha has been called "the first novel" by many literary scholars. It was published in two parts, the first in 1605 and the second in 1615. It might be viewed as a parody of chivalric romances such as Le Morte d'Arthur.

Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince (1513) is counted among the enduringly influential works of political and social philosophy from the early modern period. It appeared alongside other landmark books of the age, such as Thomas More's Utopia in 1515.

Plays meant for entertainment, rather than religious enlightenment, returned to Europe's stages in the early modern period. Among the playwrights who made important contributions were Pedro Calderón de la Barca and Lope de Vega, alongside Shakespeare, Molière and others.

Miguel de Cervantes famously burlesqued chivalric romances in his novel Don Quixote. By around 1600 these stories of knights, quests and marvel-filled adventures had gone out of fashion. Even so, the modern image of "medieval" is more influenced by romance than by any other medieval genre.

In his 1504 Libretto apologetico delle donne, the Renaissance humanist Bernardino Cacciante became the first Italian to defend Cleopatra's reputation. He criticized the moralizing and misogyny he saw in the works of Giovanni Boccaccio.

From the 16th to the 18th century, commedia dell'arte performers improvised in the streets of Italy and France. Some of these plays were written down, and both the written plays and the improvisation influenced the literature of the time, particularly the work of Molière.

Niccolò Machiavelli and Francesco Guicciardini were the chief originators of the science of history. They belonged to the 16th-century era that followed the end of the Renaissance in Italy, when writers perfected the Italian character of their language.

Pietro Bembo was an influential figure in the development of the Italian language. He worked in the 16th century, an era whose fundamental characteristic was that it perfected the Italian character of its language.

In 1690, the Academy of Arcadia was instituted with the goal of "restoring" literature. It aimed to do so by imitating the simplicity of the ancient shepherds, using forms such as sonnets and madrigals.

During the 17th century, Italy witnessed the development of the Baroque novel. Alberto Asor Rosa has suggested that it came about through the secularization of chivalric poetry and the increasingly literary character of the novella.

The Academy of Arcadia was founded in Rome at the end of the 17th century, when 14 men of letters from the circle of Queen Christina of Sweden met at a convent beside San Pietro in Montorio. It grew into a literary movement that spread across Italy in the 18th century in response to the "Baroque taste", which many critics thought bizarre, eccentric and artificial.

Giovanni Paolo Marana's Letters Writ by a Turkish Spy (1684) was one of the first epistolary novels and a best-seller of the late seventeenth century. It influenced Montesquieu in writing the Persian Letters (1721), and Daniel Defoe wrote an unofficial sequel in 1718.
tags: Letters Writ by a Turkish Spy

literature.text: Giovanni Ambrogio Marini presented an idealization of aristocratic life in his highly successful Calloandro fedele (1640–1). In a radical move, Girolamo Brusoni's Trilogia di Glisomiro (1657–62) replaced the lives and loves of the aristocracy with those of the contemporary bourgeoisie.
Pace Pasini's L'historia del cavalier perduto (1644) combines chivalric, picaresque, and political themes. It was likely a source for Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed.

science.text: Galileo Galilei's early 17th-century telescopic observations began a transformation in astronomy. What had been a narrowly technical revision of classical astronomy became an increasingly aggressive challenge to traditional cosmology and its long-standing synthesis with Christian theology.

One of the most important technological developments of the Renaissance was the caravel. It combined European and North African ship building technologies, and for the first time made extensive trade and travel over the Atlantic feasible.
In 1600, Giordano Bruno was burned alive at Campo de' Fiori in Rome after being convicted of heresy. He was an Italian philosopher, poet, alchemist, astronomer and cosmological theorist.

Boscovich and the English Jesuit Christopher Maire measured an arc of two degrees of the meridian between Rome and Rimini. The work began at the end of 1750 and took about two years. An account was published in 1755, accompanied by a carefully prepared map of the States of the Church.

The caravel was first introduced by the Italian states and early captains such as Giovanni Caboto, Giovanni da Verrazzano and Columbus, who were Italian explorers. Its development would end Northern Italy's role as the trade crossroads of Europe, shifting wealth and power westwards to Portugal, Spain, France, England, and the Netherlands.

politics.text: After the Peace of Cateau Cambrésis in 1559, France renounced its claims in Italy. Powerful dynasties ruled several Italian states: the Medici in Tuscany, the Farnese in Parma, the Este in Modena, and the Savoy in Piedmont.

Nearly half of Italy was ruled by the Spanish Empire, including the kingdoms of Naples, Sicily and Sardinia and the Duchy of Milan. As Spain declined in the 16th century, so did these Italian possessions.

In 1556 Charles V divided the House of Habsburg, ceding Austria and the Imperial crown to his brother Ferdinand and the Spanish Empire to his son Philip. The Spanish branch also held the Netherlands, the Kingdom of Portugal between 1580 and 1640, and the Mezzogiorno of Italy.

Naples was one of Europe's most overcrowded and unsanitary cities, with a crime-ridden and volatile populace. Its aristocracy long resented Spanish rule and welcomed the Austrians in 1707, but was disappointed when Vienna kept denying Naples any autonomy. While the war raged, Austria imposed huge tax burdens on the city and provided no adequate administration until peace returned.

In 1734 the Spanish-born Don Carlos ascended the throne of a reborn Kingdom of Naples. In 1759 he left to become King Charles III of Spain, and his underage son Ferdinand succeeded him with the regent Bernardo Tanucci governing.

From 1580 to 1640 the Portuguese and Spanish Empires were joined in a personal union of their Habsburg monarchs, known as the Iberian Union. Beneath the highest level of government, their separate administrations were maintained.

During its Siglo de Oro, the Spanish Empire held Mexico, South America, the Philippines and all of southern Italy. It also held a stretch of territories from the Duchy of Milan to the Netherlands, giving it a global presence.

Bernardo Tanucci tried to build a benevolent despotism in the spirit of the Enlightenment. When Ferdinand came of age in 1767 he showed little interest in government, and his wife Maria Carolina replaced Tanucci with Sir John Acton, an English emigre.

The Spanish branch of the Habsburgs, which held all of Iberia and lands in Italy, became extinct in the male line in 1700. The dynasty nonetheless continued through the female line, through the House of Bourbon.

The Italian Gonzaga family claimed a share of the Byzantine legacy as matrilineal descendants of the Palaeologus-Montferrat family. Vincenzo II Gonzaga (1594–1627) and Charles I Gonzaga (1580–1637) both aspired to lead crusades against the Ottomans to restore the Byzantine Empire and claim its throne.
Andreas Palaiologos held titular rights to the Byzantine throne until he bequeathed them to Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain in 1502. This gave the Spanish monarchs a paper claim to a vanished empire.

Nicolaus Copernicus dedicated De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres) to Pope Paul III, who held the papal throne from 1534 to 1549. Paul III became the grandfather of Alessandro Farnese.

Cardinal Michael Friedrich von Althann, viceroy of Naples from 1722 to 1728, tried to found a state bank, the Banco di San Carlo, to acquire crown lands for the Austrian emperor. The plan infuriated both the nobility and the middle class, and after his expulsion Naples suffered famine and social unrest.

philosophy.text: In 1600, the Italian philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned alive at Campo de' Fiori in Rome after being convicted of heresy. Bruno was also an poet, alchemist, astronomer, cosmological theorist and esotericist.
In 1633 the Roman Inquisition found Galileo "vehemently suspect of heresy" after he defended heliocentricism. His defence challenged the traditional Aristotelian cosmology of the time.

Franciscus Patricius was born in 1529 on Cres and was a philosopher and scientist from the Republic of Venice. He defended Platonism and opposed Aristotelianism. Sources describe him as both Croatian and Italian.
In 1611 Federico Cesi founded the first Accademia dei Lincei. Its discussions rejected the traditional Aristotelian framework.

Patricius first studied Aristotelian philosophy at the University of Padua, but he turned to Platonism while still a student. He then became a sharp, high-profile opponent of Aristotelianism and grappled with it extensively in several writings.

After years of unsuccessful efforts to secure a livelihood, Patricius was invited in 1577 to the ducal court of the House of Este in Ferrara. At the University of Ferrara, a chair for Platonic philosophy was set up especially for him.

Patricius planned his main work, the Nova de universis philosophia, in eight parts. He completed only the first four and published them in Ferrara in 1591. He dedicated that first edition to Pope Gregory XIV, a friend from his childhood in Padua.

Pierre Gassendi had wanted to write a book against Aristotelianism, but he gave up the project when he discovered Patricius's Nova de universis philosophia. His concept of space clearly shows the influence of that work.

Patricius worked on another part of his great project, De humana philosophia, in 1591 and 1592. The manuscript stayed incomplete, because a conflict with the censorship authority prevented its completion and publication.

The English natural philosopher Nicholas Hill took up Patricius's ideas in his Philosophia Epicurea, printed in 1601, without naming him. Pierre Bayle later said that the Nova de universis philosophia reveals the very admirable depth of mind of its author.

culture.text: On 6 May 1527, mutinous, largely unpaid troops of Charles V broke into the scarcely defended city of Rome and began looting, killing and holding citizens for ransom without any restraint. Women were raped, hospice patients killed, and monks castrated and nuns raped, and an estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people were murdered. Rome's population fell from 55,000 to 10,000 because of the atrocities, famine, plague and flight from the city.

After the sack of Rome, in which an estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people were murdered, Charles V came to terms with Pope Clement VII. The Church shifted from Renaissance freethought toward the orthodoxy of the Counter-Reformation. Under the influence of Charles and later Philip II of Spain, the Inquisition became pervasive, and Renaissance humanism came to be viewed as contrary to Church teachings.

Between 1656 and 1667, Gian Lorenzo Bernini redesigned the open space before Saint Peter's Basilica under Pope Alexander VII. It was designed so that the greatest number of people could see the Pope give his blessing.

The Val Camonica witch trials were two large witch trials held in 1505 to 1510 and 1518 to 1521, among the biggest in Italy. Each trial caused the deaths of about 60 people, 110 in total. The best source is considered to be the Venetian Marin Sanudo, chronicler to the Council of Ten from 1496 to 1536. Giacinto Gaggia, the bishop of Brescia, ordered the documentary evidence destroyed to stop the anticlerical opposition from using it.

The first newspaper printed in Rome was the Diario Ordinario, established by the Chracas family in 1716. It marked the beginning of regular news publications in the town, though other newspapers printed in the Papal States were already circulating in Rome before then.

Benvenuto Cellini witnessed the 1527 sack of Rome and described it in his works. He claimed in his own account to have shot the Duke of Bourbon dead during the assault. In the sack, an estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people were murdered, and it is said two thousand bodies were thrown into the Tiber River. Charles V later restored many of the spoils, worth more than 4 million ducati, to the Vatican.
